sources.title: Pirc Defense overview, 150 Attack and Austrian Attack (search snippets only)

overview: Black plays 1...d6 and, after 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3, ...g6 and ...Bg7, letting White build the broad e4-d4 centre and then undermining it from the flanks with ...c5 or ...e5 (hypermodern: the bigger White's centre, the bigger the target). The root is a crossroads: 1...d6 can transpose to the Philidor (3...e5 or ...c6) or to the Modern. White's replies run from sharp (Austrian Attack 4.f4, 150 Attack 4.Be3 with Qd2, Bh6 and h4-h5, Byrne 4.Bg5, Bayonet h4) to unhurried (Classical 4.Nf3 with Be2 and castling, fianchetto). Typical play is imbalanced: White gets space and often a kingside attack, Black gets a solid fianchettoed king and counterplay on the queenside and with central breaks. It is sound but has a reputation for giving White chances; Kasparov doubted it for the top level (s1), though Caruana, Anand and Grischuk have used it (s2).

white_ideas.idea: Austrian Attack (4.f4): the broad pawn centre, aiming for the e5 breakthrough; the sharpest, most aggressive treatment.
150 Attack (4.Be3, Qd2, 0-0-0, Bh6, h4-h5, or f3/f4 ideas): a kingside pawn storm needing modest theory.
Classical system (4.Nf3, Be2, 0-0): unhurried, positionally sound control of the centre without over-committing.
Byrne (4.Bg5): pressure with Qd2 and Bh6 combinations.

black_ideas.idea: Allow White the centre, then strike with ...c5 or ...e5 to undermine d4, with the g7 bishop pressuring it.
Queenside expansion with ...a6, ...b5 and ...c5; the ...Nc6-a5-c4 manoeuvre.
Dark-square control from a fianchettoed kingside; make sure the Nf6 has a retreat square on d7 or e7 after White's e5.
Flexible transpositions: 3...c6 (Czech) or 3...e5 / Nbd7 can reach Philidor-type structures.

typical_structures.structure: Black pawns on d6 and g6 with a fianchettoed bishop on g7; White holds the e4-d4 duo and often castles queenside against the 150 Attack.
Austrian Attack: White f4/e4/d4 broad centre; Black counters with ...c5 or ...e5 after the tension resolves, often with doubled or isolated f-pawns possible.
Classical: solid fianchetto against an e4/d4 centre, with ...e5 or ...c5 as the break; closed-ish and manoeuvring.

character.notes: Mixed, but leans sharp and double-edged. Chessable calls it 'sharp and counter-attacking' (s2). Wikipedia describes a dynamic, unbalanced fight with a deliberately conceded centre (s1). The Austrian Attack is 'the sharpest, most aggressive way' to meet it and the 150 Attack pursues a kingside pawn storm (s3, s2). The Classical system is calmer. Risks for Black: a weakened kingside after ...h6 and ...g5 and passivity if the knight retreats badly (s2). Black's king side is solid structurally but the position can become a race. Tentatively sharp or balanced; weighed against the Modern, the Pirc is more forcing because of White's aggressive set-ups.

gambit.notes: No gambit at the root. Sidelines with a pawn sacrifice exist (Bayonet h4 sharp lines, 4.f4 Bg7 5.Nf3 c5 lines) but no material is offered in the main lines.

soundness.notes: Sound but not a favourite at the very top. Kasparov said it is 'hardly worth using in the highest category' tournaments, as it gives White 'too many opportunities' (s1, via Wikipedia). Still viable: it became respectable after the war and has been played by Grischuk, Caruana and Anand (s1, s2). So objectively playable for Black, with some practical risk. Not Dubious.

structure.notes: White gets a large pawn centre; Black allows it and challenges with ...c5 or ...e5. The centre typically stays tense with White having e4/d4, and many middlegames are closed or semi-closed until the break comes. Classical lines are closed-ish (e4/d4 vs d6/g6); sharp lines open after ...c5 and the e5 break. Judged on the typical middlegame: tense centre, mostly closed or semi-open. The sources do not label it directly (my own reading).

approach.notes: A defence to 1.e4, not played against everything, but its fianchetto-and-d6 set-up resembles a flexible system. Moderately represented at master level, a secondary choice or specialist weapon (s1); used by Grischuk, Caruana, Anand (s2). Standard rather than offbeat.

level.notes: Judged for Black. Chessable rates it moderate: principles (dark-square control, ...e5 and ...c5 levers, knight retreat squares) matter more than rote memory, though 4.Bg5 and the Austrian Attack require accurate defence (s2). Wikipedia: theory load moderate; the 150 Attack minimises White's memorisation, while the flexibility of move orders makes understanding more important than memorising (s1). So understanding rather than memory, Intermediate-leaning.

sublines_that_differ.name: Austrian Attack
sublines_that_differ.how: Sharpest and most aggressive White set-up; heavily theoretical and tactical.

sublines_that_differ.name: 150 Attack
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 d6 2. d4 Nf6 3. Nc3 g6 4. Be3
sublines_that_differ.how: Qd2, Bh6 and kingside pawn storm; modest theory, sharp middlegames, often opposite-side castling.

sublines_that_differ.name: Classical System
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 d6 2. d4 Nf6 3. Nc3 g6 4. Nf3
sublines_that_differ.how: Quieter and more positional, with Be2 and castling.

sublines_that_differ.name: Czech Defence / transpositions
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 d6 2. d4 Nf6 3. Nc3 c6
sublines_that_differ.how: Reaches Philidor-type structures instead of the Pirc fianchetto.

sublines_that_differ.name: 1...d6 2.Nf3 and Modern transpositions
sublines_that_differ.how: Move-order lines that can reach Pirc, Philidor or Modern; the subtree includes many such transpositions.

description.claim: The Pirc is a hypermodern and ambitious response to 1.e4 where Black allows White to build a large pawn centre before challenging it from the flanks.
It leads to complex, unbalanced, and often sharp middlegames.
description.note: Described as sharp and counter-attacking; the Austrian and 150 Attacks are sharp. The Classical system is calmer.

description.claim: It requires a deep understanding of counter-attacking principles.
It is ideal for flexible and resilient players who are comfortable defending under pressure.
description.note: Black often defends against a kingside attack before counterplay arrives.

common_plans.claim: Black: undermine White's centre with pawn breaks like ...c5 or ...e5 after completing development with ...Nf6 and ...g6/...Bg7.
White: seize a space advantage, build a strong pawn centre and often launch a kingside attack (e.g. the Austrian Attack with f4).
common_plans.note: Austrian Attack and 150 Attack pursue this.

common_plans.claim: Black: create queenside counterplay with moves like ...a6 and ...b5.
common_plans.note: Queenside expansion with ...a6, ...b5, ...c5 is a named plan.

common_plans.claim: White: restrict Black's pieces, control key squares and convert the space advantage into an attack or a positional bind.
common_plans.note: Broad but consistent with the Classical and attacking set-ups.
